en: Sixty thoughts came at once:
“My dear orphan,
Seen today, gone tomorrow—
Such is this world of shit.
Orphan, listen to my words.
In those days, when my caravan Manas lived,
In a Kyrgyz cap of blue-gray lynx fur,
When I tossed my head,
Knowing the world,
When I lived in delight,
Lying on my back, acting like God,
I would slice and eat rump meat.
When my soul's companion Manas lived,
I would say, ‘Where is the angel of death for me?’
After that Manas died,
I was humiliated, herding camels.
While his lord was alive,
Your elder, Lord Bakai—
The marten cap upon his head,
Who did not wear it and toss his head?
When they heard of your elder, Khan Bakai,
Great China, the khakan's people,
The mighty peoples trembled.
My dear orphan,
When I reckon up my past,
My heart is sorely troubled,
Tears spill from my eyes.
The overturned, treacherous world
Seems to have gone without a backward glance.
The goodness that lay before me,
I failed to see it.
Bruised black and blue, wretched man,
While fierce Manas was alive,
I failed to die.
Kara-Shaar and Kambil,
When I held them in my grasp,
The multitude of Manchus, the countless Torguts,
When I struck them down,
In the time of the wide world,
While my fierce one was alive,
Why did I not die then?
Narkesken, that strikes men down,
When I held it,
Upon the world, turmoil—
When I brought it,
When sacred power rested upon my head,
While Manas was safe and well,
Why did I not die then?
In those days, when I wore a shot-proof coat,
The eighteen thousand worlds,
When I trod them down like charcoal,
Why did I not die then?
Upon those I aimed at, turmoil—
When I brought it,
When from many lands
I was taking tribute,
A battle-axe with a golden cheek
Upon my arm, poor soul,
When I had it hanging there,
When the whole wide world
Was under my command,
When, devastating the world,
I swept across it,
When a throne like a camel at the place of honor
Was mine to mount,
When all the peoples with their rulers
Were mine to marshal,
Why did I not die then?
When my mighty warrior was still alive,
I broke through Ombo and took spoils,
Broke through its midst and opened a road,
Herded white deer as cattle,
Threw the places I fought into confusion,
To a pass six months’ journey away,
When my name reached there,
When to the whole wide world
My appeal could reach,
Why did I not die then?
When bored, we shot roe deer,
When not, we lay at ease,
When those great days of plenty
Were upon us,
When the laughing Kyrgyz and many Argyn
Were settled there,
When by day there was kumis, by night girls,
And such was our life,
Why did I not die then?
Here along the Talas,
When we laid out an ordo game of forty foot-lengths,
And shot the knucklebones for sport,
When a golden-mouthed trumpet
Was played by a man of mirth,
And a drum with a golden tuft
Was beaten to entertain,
Noble Manas was still there,
When a fat lamb and its tasty head
Were set to boil heartily,
When bored, we shot roe deer,
When not, here in Talas
We played at liberty,
Why did I not die then?
When my blood-shedding Manas lived,
There was the place he piled his treasury.
If I speak of my former days,
It seems as though I boast—
That wretched Bakay is me.
When your father Manas lived,
When his honor was at its height,
My dear orphan,
This was the land your father made his home.
After your father passed away,
This wretched land lay deserted.
When Manas, my twin, was here,
Here was the dark eye of the spring,
Here was the plane tree itself.
My dear orphan,
Listen closely to my words!
The bluish hillock lies in haze—
His crooked little ears stood up;
The plain ahead is visible,
Your poor uncle Bakay's heart is troubled.
There is the facing side of Bar-Kol,
And visible this side of it,
There is the garden King Manas planted.
The blue hill in gray haze—
There is the throne King Manas mounted."
Telling at length of all his deeds,
Your uncle, King Bakay,
Was all but dying now.
"I would go into the earth, but the ground is hard;
I would die, but life is sweet.
The plane tree has been felled,
Hardship has descended on me,
This damned, faithless world—
Grief weighs down my precious soul.
My long-awaited little one,
For twelve years I herded camels,
I wished to die of shame,
Yet I did not die—what could I do?—
Because you lived, my orphan.
When I remember Manas Khan,
My ribs are cruelly torn apart,
My tears pour down.
This damned, wretched life
Seems all the sweeter to my eyes.
The house built crosswise—
When I remember Manas,
Grief weighs down my wretched soul.
When my king Manas lived,
When all my wealth was mine,
This hill on which we two now stand—
My orphan foal, listen—
This is where the story springs from:
The golden throne your khan father mounted,
A garden of plane trees all around.
Beneath the golden throne,
Here is the tale of it:
Even if soaked in water forty years,
They would neither change their color nor decay;
Even if cast in water eighty years,
It would not fray, rot, or fade.
Carpets with golden patterns,
Sixty of them were spread.
Upon those carpets,
At their edges on all four sides,
Was where they gripped and swung their maces,
Was where the great guards stood.
They never saw an enemy's face;
When my blood-shedder lived,
No stranger came and went.
If you ask about this place,
It was Kanykey's white palace,
Its gate of iron, solid metal,
So many guards stood at its door.
The faithless world has passed away—
Damn it, what bliss there was!
Within that palace,
The guards were beyond counting,
The champions were more numerous still.
No one got word of what was there;
Into that palace
No mortal went visiting.
When someone touched the threshold,
The kettledrum was struck,
And farther within,
More guards were stationed,
Who swarmed together at the alarm.
Human noses and ears
They wore as amulets.
Those whom your father's hand had not touched,
Some mortals, had survived unharmed.
When Manas, my twin, died,
When my hapless soul met hardship,
Abyke, Kobosh, the six scoundrels,
Plundered and divided all my wealth.
When they plundered my costly cloth,
When the dogs stirred up trouble,
Your father's golden throne
They badly wrecked.
Binding pinewood spears together,
They made war on the golden throne,
Saying, "Manas's name shall not remain!"
Forever bellowing,
Saying, "That fool's name shall not remain!"
They felled all the plane trees,
Uprooted the pillars and let water loose,
Thus brought the palace down,
Cut down its trees and laid them low,
Toppled and demolished its buildings,
Left it utterly flat,
Thus brought it to its end.
They settled along the valley.
When the blood-shedder passed away,
Damn it, the desolate palace
Was like a fire gone out.
They did their villainy—
Abyke, Kobosh, the six scoundrels
Took their revenge upon the palace."
Seeing this, mighty Bakay,
His two eyes darting wildly,
Swooned and hung limp.
The land left by his father—
Showing the way, gathering an army,
Crying, "My tiger Manas, why did you die?"
Your uncle Bakay of many deeds
Let out a ringing wail.
Finished in anger,
His heart was heavy with grief,
He raised his voice and moaned.
Holy Bakay, the precious lion,
Then broke into ringing sobs.
If you ask of his former days,
He was known as Bakay the hero.
His black eyes, like a saker falcon's,
Filled with tears without blinking.
"All your world was left in disgrace.
You who pledged allegiance to twelve spiritual masters,
My holy Manas, take me with you!
Alas, Manas, why did you die?
Why must Bakay suffer such humiliation?
If God creates a living soul,
May such a calamity
Never be given to His mortal creature!
My dear orphan,
Your father Manas was a lion,
Who threw the whole world into turmoil,
A lion born above the rest.
A mortal like your father—
The one God, creator of life,
Will surely not grant another soon.
Before Mecca,
Your khan father was its support.
Islam stretched far and still—
That was your khan father's land.
Your father Manas, bringer of good fortune,
Was a mighty heroic support.
